title: C as an inspectable starting point

readings.purpose: Performance-awareness motivation
Notice work before trying to improve it
Separate intuitive machine stories from C rules

readings.resource: [Handmade Chat 013: Translation Units, Function Pointers, Compilation, Linking, and Execution](https://guide.handmadehero.org/chat/chat013/)
readings.purpose: Compilation and linking; adapt Windows/C++ discussion to C11/Linux
Primary authority for language/library claims
POSIX timer contract, outside ISO C

E01.title: Values and their ranges
E01.why: Your program can print a plausible number even when the format string describes the wrong type. This exercise connects a C value to the interface used to display it.
E01.predict: Which printed limits can you predict from C alone, and which require this implementation?
E01.steps: Match each argument to its format before writing the call. Read the limits from the header; test endpoints without stepping beyond them.
E01.hint: A format string is part of the function call's contract, not decoration.
E01.evidence: A successful print establishes that case. An observed wrap of a signed value would not establish a language rule.
E01.prerequisites: types, signed versus unsigned ranges, and matching a printf format to its argument

E02.title: Size and array extent
E02.why: You need a reliable way to count elements before traversing them. An array object remembers its extent in its type; a pointer parameter does not.
E02.predict: Change five elements to three on paper. Which sizes should change and which should stay fixed?
E02.steps: Write the array measurement in the scope where the complete array type is visible. Trace what is actually passed to the helper. Restore the required fixture after experimenting.
E02.hint: Keep units visible: bytes divided by bytes per element gives elements.
E02.evidence: Explain why the quotient works here before treating it as an array-length idiom everywhere.
E02.prerequisites: objects, arrays, sizeof, and the distinction between a pointer and its target

E03.title: A bounded loop
E03.why: A loop is easier to trust when you can state what its partial result means. The bound also lets you justify the arithmetic type before running it.
E03.predict: For N=3, write the running sum at each iteration; for N=0, predict how many additions occur.
E03.steps: Validate the input first. Choose an invariant about the already-processed prefix, then test entry, progress, and exit separately.
E03.hint: The empty prefix has a useful sum even though no loop body executes.
E03.evidence: Passing four examples is evidence; the invariant and range bound explain the whole permitted domain.
E03.prerequisites: loop invariants, output pointers, and a bounded integer range

E04.title: Status and output
E04.why: A failed clamp needs to report failure without inventing a number that could also be a valid answer. This introduces a status return alongside an output object.
E04.predict: Put a sentinel in the output and predict its value after reversed endpoints.
E04.steps: Separate validation from the three valid regions. Test equality at both boundaries and a one-point interval.
E04.hint: Check the interval before deciding where the value lies.
E04.evidence: An unchanged output on failure is observable API behavior, just as much as the successful clamp.
E04.prerequisites: inclusive intervals and a status separate from the returned value

E05.title: An aggregate result
E05.why: An array summary contains several facts that belong together. A struct groups those facts, while a status distinguishes an empty input from a meaningful minimum.
E05.predict: Try an all-positive array and an all-negative array with an initial minimum of zero.
E05.steps: Establish the empty policy first. For nonempty input, initialize from a real element and trace how each later element updates the extrema.
E05.hint: An arbitrary initial zero is not a member of every dataset.
E05.evidence: Use the status to interpret the fields. The zero fields of an empty result do not claim that its minimum is zero.
E05.prerequisites: arrays, structs, and the special meaning of an empty input

E06.title: Two ways through one array
E06.why: Indexing and pointer traversal are two ways to name elements. Relating them makes pointer arithmetic less mysterious without claiming a particular machine implementation.
E06.predict: Predict the sum after changing the first element from 4 to 5. Draw the final legal one-past position.
E06.steps: Track which element each expression names and establish the sum bound. Handle the empty NULL case before doing pointer arithmetic.
E06.hint: Advancing an int pointer moves by one int, not one byte.
E06.evidence: Equal sums show semantic agreement on the inputs. They do not prove equal generated instructions or equal execution time.
E06.prerequisites: array bounds, pointer arithmetic, and a running sum

E07.title: Coordinates as a contract
E07.why: A pair of floating-point numbers is not automatically a usable location. Units, finiteness, and geographic bounds give the fields meaning.
E07.predict: What does a rejection test using only less-than and greater-than do with NaN?
E07.steps: State units beside each field. Check finiteness before reasoning about interval membership. Test poles, longitude endpoints, and invalid values separately.
E07.hint: NaN does not behave like an ordinary number outside an interval.
E07.evidence: A valid coordinate is an accepted representation under this API; it does not prove that the location was measured accurately.
E07.prerequisites: struct members, units, and passing a value to a function

E08.title: Struct layout
E08.why: A char, a double, and an int need not fit into the sum of their individual sizes. The compiler must also place objects at suitable boundaries.
E08.predict: Draw both field orders, including the last element of a two-element array of each struct.
E08.steps: Use offsets and member sizes to mark occupied spans. Attribute the remaining positions to padding rather than reading arbitrary bytes for a pattern.
E08.hint: Tail padding helps the next array element meet its alignment.
E08.evidence: Your diagram describes the observed layout. A different compiler target may choose another valid layout, and smaller size alone says nothing about speed.
E08.prerequisites: member offsets, padding, and unsigned-byte inspection

E09.title: Seeing representation
E09.why: A number's printed hexadecimal value and its stored byte order are different views. Character access lets you inspect the latter without pretending it has another object type.
E09.predict: Write the two familiar byte orders for the specified value before printing either.
E09.steps: Read through unsigned characters, retain CHAR_BIT and sizeof in the report, then compare only arrangements supported by those observations.
E09.hint: The first byte in memory need not contain the most significant digits you wrote in source.
E09.evidence: Report the bytes and the classification separately. This is an implementation observation, not a promise that every C machine has four 8-bit bytes here.
E09.prerequisites: a value versus its object representation, unsigned-byte access, and byte order

E10.title: Bit flags
E10.why: One unsigned value can carry several yes/no properties. The difficulty is changing one property without destroying its neighbors.
E10.predict: Predict the effect of setting twice and toggling twice, using a four-bit drawing.
E10.steps: Trace every operation against its mask. Test a combined mask so that all-bits semantics cannot accidentally become any-bit semantics.
E10.hint: Clearing requires preserving bits outside the mask.
E10.evidence: The valid shift domain is part of the reasoning. Do not execute an invalid shift to discover what the language means.
E10.prerequisites: unsigned masks, shifts, and the width of the promoted operand

E11.title: Allocation and ownership
E11.why: A requested element count must become a safe byte count before memory is requested. The returned pointer also creates a cleanup obligation.
E11.predict: For N=5, list the initialized values and total; for zero, predict whether allocation is needed.
E11.steps: Validate multiplication and the cap, allocate, check, initialize, use, then free. Follow the failure path with the same care as success.
E11.hint: An allocation is storage, not initialized values.
E11.evidence: A correct result includes cleanup and failure behavior. One successful allocation does not demonstrate that failure is impossible.
E11.prerequisites: allocated storage, ownership, and checked size multiplication

E12.title: Reading a file reliably
E12.why: The last read can mean normal completion or an error. A count is credible only if the whole input was read and the stream was closed successfully.
E12.predict: Compare an empty file, a missing file, and a file whose final byte is not a newline.
E12.steps: Keep fgetc's result in int. Count only after distinguishing EOF, check ferror, and close every successfully opened stream.
E12.hint: Do not narrow the read result before deciding whether it is EOF.
E12.evidence: Bytes and newlines answer different questions. A successful prefix count cannot be returned as a successful whole-file count after an error.
E12.prerequisites: file streams, byte counts, and distinguishing an error from end-of-file

E13.title: Parsing is more than conversion
E13.why: A conversion function understands a language of its own. Your API accepts a narrower grammar, so a returned number is not enough.
E13.predict: List strings that strtoull accepts but this exercise must reject.
E13.steps: Validate the digit-only grammar, reset and inspect errno for the conversion, inspect the end pointer, then apply the application limit.
E13.hint: Separate malformed text from a well-formed number that is too large.
E13.evidence: Acceptance means the complete string met the declared contract, not that a numeric prefix was found.
E13.prerequisites: decimal digits, accumulation, and checking before multiplication

E14.title: Separate compilation
E14.why: A caller can know a function's interface before the linker finds its implementation. This explains why a program can compile and still fail to link.
E14.predict: Draw the two object files and mark which defines count_equal and which refers to it.
E14.steps: Read the header, implement the definition in its own source, compile separately, and compare object symbols with executable symbols.
E14.hint: An include guard prevents repeated inclusion in one translation unit, not definitions in several object files.
E14.evidence: The symbol listing is tool evidence. Connect each entry to the C declaration or definition that caused it.
E14.prerequisites: declarations, definitions, translation units, and linkage

E15.title: Timing as an experiment
E15.why: One duration is a measurement, not a property of the source. Correctness and an explicit timed region make a small benchmark interpretable.
E15.predict: State whether you expect the optimized build to be faster and why the expectation might fail.
E15.steps: Initialize and warm up outside timing. Verify checksums, record five trials, sort copies for statistics, and preserve raw results.
E15.hint: The volatile reads make this particular experiment observable but also constrain what it models.
E15.evidence: Discuss overhead and variation before comparing builds. The tests deliberately do not require a speedup.
E15.prerequisites: elapsed time, repeated observations, and the difference between equivalent results and equivalent work

guidance.P01: This classification exercise separates rules from tempting machine stories. For each claim, identify the operation and its type before deciding which authority could justify it.
guidance.P02: Use units to make the array/pointer distinction visible. Predict both measurements first; the pointer spelling avoids a warning without changing what the parameter means.
guidance.P03: Trace the loop on paper, including its final iteration. The purpose is to detect the invalid access from the bound, not to hope a crash will reveal it.
guidance.P04: Use the layout process from E08. Keep your target-specific prediction separate from the relationships a portable test may require.
guidance.P05: Draw artifacts rather than a single box called compiler. Follow the function name through each stage to locate the missing-definition error.
guidance.P06: Ask what work is inside the clock readings and what result remains observable. Each defective benchmark changes the question being measured.
guidance.S01: Stretch: choose a short loop and annotate operands before instruction names. Compare two actual listings from your toolchain, then state what timing information is still absent.
guidance.S02: Stretch: first decide what a logical line means. Use the final unterminated line to show why newline count alone is insufficient.
guidance.R01: A reader needs your build context to interpret sizes and timings. Record commands as run, not the flags you intended to use.
guidance.R02: Keep your original predictions visible. A failed prediction followed by a careful explanation is more informative than a rewritten correct guess.
guidance.R03: Choose observations with a useful contrast: a measured byte count versus a guaranteed relationship, for example. Use the standard terminology precisely.
guidance.R04: Preserve the raw trials so another reader can reproduce your statistics. Explain the timed region before interpreting the comparison.
guidance.R05: Make the handoff sufficient to repeat the work. Choose a mechanism that would still matter when expressed through a different language.

companion.title: Chapter 14: Types II: Way More Types

E01.title: Bytes without losing the value
E01.why: To inspect an object's storage, you need a byte view that does not invent a different object type. Formatting adds its own capacity contract.
E01.predict: Count the characters needed for four hex bytes, including spaces and the final terminator.
E01.steps: Validate sizes before multiplication or reads, inspect with unsigned characters, and commit only after the destination can hold everything.
E01.hint: The last byte needs a terminator where an earlier byte needs a separator.
E01.evidence: A representation dump is evidence about bytes. Equal field values need not imply equal padding bytes.
E01.prerequisites: unsigned bytes, object extents, and bounded output

E02.title: Alignment as a numeric boundary
E02.why: Rounding a size up is useful when the next object must begin at a particular boundary. At the integer limit, the rounding operation itself can fail.
E02.predict: For alignment eight, predict the rounded positions of 0, 1, 8, and 9.
E02.steps: First validate the alignment, then reason about the extra distance to the boundary. Test the largest valid result and the next request.
E02.hint: Make the overflow check precede the addition that would overflow.
E02.evidence: The arithmetic can be portable even when the table of actual type alignments is platform-specific.

E03.title: Predicting a layout
E03.why: A model is useful because you can compare its prediction with a compiler's layout. It needs an explicit rule, not a memorized offset.
E03.predict: Draw the synthetic three-field layout and a reordered A before calling the inspector.
E03.steps: Advance a running end through aligned member positions, then round the final size. Validate the full request before writing offsets.
E03.hint: A late invalid member must not leave earlier offsets changed.
E03.evidence: Agreement supports this layout model on the target. It does not make the model a universal C struct-layout algorithm.
E03.prerequisites: aligned offsets, member spans, and the final array stride

E04.title: Drawing occupied spans
E04.why: A printed byte value cannot tell you whether its location belongs to a member or padding. Offsets and extents can.
E04.predict: Predict how adding a char after the int changes A's map and whether its total size grows.
E04.steps: Validate each extent and every overlap before filling the map. Try an unsorted span list to separate labels from positions.
E04.hint: An Inner member occupies a top-level span that may itself contain internal padding.
E04.evidence: Explain both levels of layout. Dots identify unused top-level spans, not a particular stored byte value.
E04.prerequisites: the layout model from E03 and capacity checks before writing

E05.title: Offsets need units
E05.why: The third record's field is found using an element stride and a within-element offset. Mixing those units produces plausible but wrong addresses.
E05.predict: Compute the requested last record member and grid cell symbolically before substituting observed sizes.
E05.steps: Check total extent as well as the selected offset. Trace row-major indexing as rows passed, then columns passed.
E05.hint: A pointer step already includes the size of its pointed-to type.
E05.evidence: A legal one-past pointer is a boundary marker, not another object to access.
E05.prerequisites: array index, element stride, and member offset as different quantities

E06.title: Identity over time
E06.why: Two calls may reuse an address after an object dies. Two simultaneously live objects need distinguishable identities. Those are different claims.
E06.predict: Predict the static counter, automatic counter, and two independently allocated counters across repeated calls.
E06.steps: Draw lifetime intervals. Sequence stateful calls in separate statements and examine snapshots captured while objects are alive.
E06.hint: The local pointer variable and the allocation it points to have different lifetimes.
E06.evidence: Addresses do not prove that every local has a stack slot. Report reuse as an observation, not a language guarantee.
E06.prerequisites: automatic storage duration, lifetime, and reuse of an address

E07.title: Carving a storage block
E07.why: Enough bytes are not enough: each typed object also needs valid alignment, extent, and a legal storage basis.
E07.predict: Sketch the header, alignment gap, and first two records before any casts.
E07.steps: Compute all required extents with checked arithmetic, validate the block, then initialize objects and publish outputs.
E07.hint: A declared character array does not become arbitrary struct storage merely because its address is aligned.
E07.evidence: Distinguish allocation ownership from carving. Only the owner releases the original block.
E07.prerequisites: aligned numeric offsets, checked bounds, and the lifetime of an allocated storage block

E08.title: References that survive copying
E08.why: Copy a pointer-linked structure and its pointer values still name the old targets. Indices can instead resolve relative to the chosen table.
E08.predict: Draw the copied 1→3→2 chain twice, once with indices and once with pointers.
E08.steps: Reserve zero, validate every reference, and bound traversal by the number of usable slots. Keep originals alive during comparisons.
E08.hint: If another nonzero step follows the usable-slot bound, some slot must repeat.
E08.evidence: Relocatability depends on preserved slot identity. Indices alone do not define a portable file format or survive arbitrary reordering.
E08.prerequisites: pointer values, copied objects, and resolving an index against a selected table

E09.title: Names across source files
E09.why: The word static has related but distinct effects at file and block scope. A symbol table helps separate visibility from persistence.
E09.predict: Classify each object's duration and linkage before looking at nm.
E09.steps: Follow declarations into definitions, compile both objects, then compare their symbols and relocations with the linked result.
E09.hint: File-scope const in C does not automatically make a name private.
E09.evidence: Section names and symbol letters are toolchain evidence; duration and linkage are language concepts.
E09.prerequisites: scope, linkage, declarations, and definitions from Week 1 E14

E10.title: Composing the inspector
E10.why: A useful command is a sequence of contracts: parse a request, predict layout, allocate output, and render it. Failures must compose too.
E10.predict: Draw both requested field orders and predict their sizes before running the command.
E10.steps: Retain the supplied parser, copy the checked helpers, and follow ownership through every later error path.
E10.hint: A trusted helper does not remove the caller's duty to satisfy its preconditions.
E10.evidence: The explanation of a prediction mismatch is the learning outcome. Merely reporting the tool's result does not show how the layout arose.
E10.prerequisites: the checked layout and rendering helpers from E01–E05

guidance.P01: For each claim, name the object, storage, or pointer involved. Some statements confuse an observed layout with a guarantee; others make an invalid inference from byte contents.
guidance.P02: Draw a timeline for each object. Fill the linkage column independently: a name being visible across files and an object remaining alive are different properties.
guidance.P03: Treat the supplied size/alignment pairs as the model input. Compute on paper before asking your machine; a different actual ABI does not invalidate a correct synthetic calculation.
guidance.P04: Write the pointer types beside the expressions. Element differences and byte distances have different units, and legal formation is not the same as legal dereference.
guidance.P05: Compare declared type with allocated storage before considering alignment. Repair the invalid approach by choosing a real object or copying a valid representation, not by adding a cast.
guidance.P06: Trace which table a reference resolves against after each operation. An index survives relocation only while its slot continues to represent the intended object.
guidance.S01: Stretch: distinguish field identities even when two fields have the same type. An exhaustive result for five fields and a proof for all model inputs are different deliverables.
guidance.S02: Stretch: follow one symbol from declaration to object section and relocation. Record tool versions so changed names or offsets are not mistaken for errors.
guidance.R01: Tool versions matter when you interpret symbol tables. Record the source of each environment fact rather than inferring it from a familiar-looking output.
guidance.R02: Draw first, then compare. Keep nested padding separate from the padding around the nested member, and retain every failed prediction.
guidance.R03: The ledger is an exercise in choosing the right authority. A compiler observation cannot establish a portable C requirement.
guidance.R04: Connect the videos to the concrete block and reference experiments you performed. State the legality conditions before transferring a design from C++ to C.
guidance.R05: Record the time you actually needed. The course estimate is a planning hypothesis, and the next question should follow from an unresolved observation.

readings.purpose: The problem the whole year returns to: what is computed, over what inputs, with which formula. The paid episode has its own constants and data; this week uses its own.
Length, normalization and the zero-length case; direction versus magnitude.
Parametric intersection, the divide-by-zero (parallel) case, and a floating-point failure in geometry code.
Coordinate bases and the dot product as measurement.
Origins and basis vectors described in terms of others.
Language authority, distinct from what IEC 60559 hardware and glibc do.

readings.resource: [Goldberg, What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html)
readings.portion: Rounding error, relative error versus ulps, guard digits
readings.purpose: Vocabulary for error measurement; read for method, not theorems.

readings.portion: The definition of the result; how math functions report errors
readings.purpose: Linux facts outside ISO C. **`fmod(3)` does not state that the result is exact**; that guarantee is in C11 Annex F. This course checks arguments itself and never relies on `errno`.

companion.title: §14.4 More Float: double and long double

E01.title: Inside a floating-point value
E01.why: A decimal display hides the finite representation that arithmetic actually uses. The fields explain both useful precision and exceptional values.
E01.predict: Predict the exponent fields of the four named numbers before inspecting them.
E01.steps: Use the platform gate, copy bytes legally, extract fields, then compose and compare the representation. Keep field-range rejection separate from value classification.
E01.hint: A normal value has an implicit leading one; a subnormal does not.
E01.evidence: The gate limits the representation claim. A NaN payload from this run is not a portable expected value.
E01.prerequisites: legal byte copying, binary64 fields, and the platform gate

E02.title: What counts as close
E02.why: One absolute tolerance cannot sensibly compare both tiny and enormous values. A useful comparison must say what error scale matters.
E02.predict: Predict the ulp gaps before running the supplied association examples.
E02.steps: Distinguish invalid tolerances from unequal values. Work through finite values, zeros, infinities, and NaNs before implementing the ordered key.
E02.hint: An ulp counts representable steps near a value, not a fixed decimal distance everywhere.
E02.evidence: A tolerance is part of the question you ask, not permission to ignore any mismatch.
E02.prerequisites: absolute error, relative error, representable steps, and exceptional values

E03.title: Angles with a declared policy
E03.why: Longitude has several equivalent descriptions, but a program benefits from one canonical interval. Conversion to radians introduces a separate approximation.
E03.predict: Sketch 179° to −179° on a circle, and predict the sign of sin(GEO_PI).
E03.steps: Separate validation, wrapping, exact quadrants, and general trigonometry. Label degrees and radians in every intermediate expression.
E03.hint: The half-open interval avoids two names for the same boundary; it is a design choice.
E03.evidence: Exact quadrant behavior follows this API's explicit branches. It is not evidence that ordinary sin of an approximate pi returns exact zero.
E03.prerequisites: degrees, radians, wrapping, and canonical boundary values

E04.title: Vectors without spurious overflow
E04.why: A finite vector can have a length too large to represent, even though its direction is perfectly usable. Length and normalization therefore need distinct contracts.
E04.predict: Compare squaring 1e200 with first dividing its components by their largest magnitude.
E04.steps: Start with the zero case, scale nonzero components, and reason separately about returning a magnitude and returning a direction. Preserve original horizontal components for longitude.
E04.hint: You need not reconstruct the enormous original length to compute a unit direction.
E04.evidence: A successful unit-vector result does not imply that the original length fits in double.
E04.prerequisites: vector components, a basis, scaling, and a zero-length vector

E05.title: Equivalent formulas, different errors
E05.why: Three mathematically equivalent distance formulas can react differently to rounding. Nearby points make the distinction visible.
E05.predict: State which formula you expect to lose information near zero distance, and by roughly how much.
E05.steps: Derive analytic expectations for simple arcs, validate coordinates, and track each formula's inverse-function input. Compare absolute error rather than matching printed digits alone.
E05.hint: Subtracting or inverting values very close to an endpoint can magnify a small input error.
E05.evidence: The sphere is already a model of Earth. Separate modeling error from input quantization and floating-point computation error.
E05.prerequisites: spherical coordinates, analytic reference cases, and cancellation

E06.title: Geometry at the boundaries
E06.why: A crossing formula with a denominator is not a complete segment-intersection algorithm. Parallel, overlapping, and zero-length segments ask different questions.
E06.predict: Draw one example of each result kind before choosing numerical coordinates.
E06.steps: Classify the geometry before dividing. Reuse an actual endpoint when required, then compare against the independent lattice oracle.
E06.hint: The bounded integer-input exactness argument does not automatically cover arbitrary noninteger coordinates.
E06.evidence: A lattice test is strong evidence for those cases; state the domain of the proof rather than generalizing from the picture.
E06.prerequisites: orientation, collinearity, endpoint inclusion, and the declared tolerance

E07.title: A library others can depend on
E07.why: The earlier files are experiments. This step gives their useful mechanisms one public interface that later weeks can call without depending on demo printing.
E07.predict: Predict which symbols belong in geomath.o's public symbol list.
E07.steps: Move declarations into the header, keep implementation helpers private, and compile the demo separately. Preserve status and output contracts across the boundary.
E07.hint: The library reports facts; the caller decides how to display them.
E07.evidence: A clean symbol boundary shows interface discipline, not proof that the math is correct. Retain the numerical tests too.
E07.prerequisites: the numerical contracts from E01–E06 and separate compilation

guidance.P01: Choose the authority before judging the equation. For a false general claim, one verified counterexample is enough; a true-looking example cannot prove a universal identity.
guidance.P02: Work in powers of two first, then translate the exponent into its stored biased form. Compare the hand result with the representation inspector only afterwards.
guidance.P03: Separate mathematical pi from GEO_PI. A local approximation near pi predicts both the sign and scale of the residual; record the prediction before libm supplies digits.
guidance.P04: Start with the geometric meaning of a dot product of unit vectors. Show each algebraic step, then mark where finite arithmetic can cross the exact interval boundary.
guidance.P05: Draw the six geometries before calculating. The pictures should force distinct branches, including cases where the generic division formula is inapplicable.
guidance.P06: Compare input resolution and arithmetic resolution in the same units. Distinguish the rounding of one coordinate from the combined error of a distance between two points.
guidance.S01: Stretch: write the intended defect next to each property. A property test is more informative when you can deliberately introduce a fault that it detects.
guidance.S02: Stretch: preserve the actual stored longitude as the reference input. Otherwise input rounding can be misreported as a distance-formula error.
guidance.R01: The floating-point flags are part of the experiment. A changed reassociation policy can change the behavior you intended to study.
guidance.R02: Numerical predictions should expose a model, not merely say close. Record a sign, a scale, or a count of representable steps before seeing the output.
guidance.R03: Distinguish the representation contract from the library implementation and its observed final digits. Name the authority for every ledger entry.
guidance.R04: Show the reference, measured result, error, and tolerance together. Explain why the tolerance is defensible for that case rather than chosen after failure.
guidance.R05: The next week introduces file quantization and many-term sums. Use your current error analysis to identify what those additions might change.

E01.title: Reproducible pseudorandom data
E01.why: A seed is useful only if the generator's update rule and output selection are specified. Otherwise two machines can start alike and produce different files.
E01.predict: Use a tiny hypothetical range to predict which residues get an extra occurrence under modulo reduction.
E01.steps: Trace the state recurrence and count every draw, including rejected draws. Keep latitude and longitude draws in separate statements.
E01.hint: Rejecting a short excess prefix leaves equally sized residue classes.
E01.evidence: Deterministic is not cryptographically random, and uniform integer coordinates are not uniform locations on a sphere.
E01.prerequisites: unsigned wraparound, deterministic state updates, and modulo bias

E02.title: Exact text from integers
E02.why: Six decimal places can be represented as an integer count of millionths. Formatting that count avoids an unnecessary round trip through binary floating point.
E02.predict: Write the exact spelling and buffer length of a negative value whose magnitude is below one degree.
E02.steps: Validate the limit, derive a safe magnitude, split whole and fractional parts, and reserve space for the terminator.
E02.hint: The sign belongs to the original value, not only to the truncated whole-degree part.
E02.evidence: An exact file spelling does not make its later double representation exact.
E02.prerequisites: integer quotient and remainder, signs, and string capacity

E03.title: A file as an observable result
E03.why: A reproducible generator must specify not only numbers but their order and exact bytes. It must also handle writes that fail late.
E03.predict: Bound the size of the 1,000-row file from its possible line lengths before generating it.
E03.steps: Compose the generator and formatter, check every write, then flush and close. Trace cleanup separately after an open failure and after a later failure.
E03.hint: Removing a partial output is appropriate only after this call actually opened the destination under the stated contract.
E03.evidence: A matching hash shows byte identity for that input. The argument about arithmetic and formatting explains why repeatability is intended.
E03.prerequisites: the generator and formatter from E01–E02, file ownership, and sequencing

E04.title: Grammar before conversion
E04.why: The parser must recognize the agreed data format, not every string a general numeric converter understands. Error order is also part of its public behavior.
E04.predict: Choose five lines with different faults and write the first expected status for each.
E04.steps: Check field count, then each field's grammar and range in the specified order. Accumulate with a pre-operation overflow guard and publish only the finished record.
E04.hint: A malformed latitude and an out-of-range latitude are different error classes.
E04.evidence: A parser's acceptance is a claim about this grammar. It is not a claim that the original observation or identifier is trustworthy.
E04.prerequisites: bounded byte input, a grammar, numeric ranges, and validate-then-commit

E05.title: Loading with bounded resources
E05.why: A file can end halfway through a record or contain a line longer than expected. A loader turns those stream events into a complete owned array or an explicit failure.
E05.predict: Draw the ownership of the file and array before and after a realloc that fails.
E05.steps: Track line number, current line extent, capacity, count, and ownership separately. Parse a row before deciding whether an otherwise-valid extra row exceeds the cap.
E05.hint: Assign realloc's result to a temporary so failure does not lose the original allocation.
E05.evidence: A partially accumulated array is not a successful whole-file result. Check close errors as well as read errors.
E05.prerequisites: the row parser, allocation growth, stream errors, and cleanup ownership

E06.title: The reference processor
E06.why: A simple implementation becomes a reference through an explicit contract and independent checks, not by being the first code written.
E06.predict: For a tiny dataset, predict which points are selected and the order of accumulation.
E06.steps: Validate inputs, preserve the required traversal order, and compare with the supplied different distance formulation. Justify the allowed discrepancy.
E06.hint: Two implementations sharing the same defect can agree. Analytic cases provide another kind of evidence.
E06.evidence: Agreement within tolerance supports the checked cases; it does not establish that either formula is uniformly accurate everywhere.
E06.prerequisites: the loaded point representation and Week 3 distance contracts

E07.title: Adding many small contributions
E07.why: Rounding happens at each operation, so the route through a sum matters. A million individually reasonable contributions can accumulate differently.
E07.predict: Predict which test inputs make naive summation lose small contributions and why changing order might matter.
E07.steps: Trace a short example by hand, then compare the prescribed naive, pairwise, and compensated methods under the fixed compiler flags.
E07.hint: Compensation records information lost by an earlier addition so later work can account for it.
E07.evidence: A worst-case bound is a limit, not a prediction that every dataset reaches it. No speed claim belongs to this week.
E07.prerequisites: rounding of additions, cancellation, and reference-based error measures

guidance.P01: Label the source of each claim. A repeated seed, unsigned arithmetic, locale, and character classification belong to different contracts and fail for different reasons.
guidance.P02: Divide the number of possible raw values by the bound and account for the remainder. That counting argument explains the bias before any statistical experiment.
guidance.P03: Count visible characters and the terminator separately. For negative fractions, retain the sign even when the whole-degree part is zero.
guidance.P04: Apply the error order as a decision procedure. A line can have several faults, but the contract selects one first diagnosis.
guidance.P05: Draw old and new allocations during a moving realloc. Peak storage can exceed the final array size, and losing the old pointer on failure loses ownership.
guidance.P06: A worst-case error bound controls risk over a class of inputs. Compare it with the measured corpus without treating a smaller observation as a refutation.
guidance.S01: Stretch: preserve operation order while changing layout. Storage accounting is permitted evidence here; cache or speed conclusions need the later measurement experiment.
guidance.S02: Stretch: label the flag-changing experiment separately from the accepted build. Preserve both commands and outcomes, including an honest absence of observed differences.
guidance.R01: The generator and oracle use different tools, so record both toolchains. Preserve exact flags for any reproducibility comparison.
guidance.R02: Your file-size and parser-status predictions exercise different models. Keep their derivations alongside the outputs, not only a pass mark.
guidance.R03: Distinguish a format promise from a libm observation. An oracle result is evidence produced by software, not an extra language standard.
guidance.R04: Name the reference used for each error calculation. Exact arithmetic and a second numerical formula provide different kinds of comparison.
guidance.R05: Prepare a handoff that lets the next week time a correct processor. The unresolved question should concern a concrete experimental control.

readings.purpose: How much work one instruction can do; why a scalar baseline is recorded now. No SIMD this week.
Why the same arithmetic can cost different amounts depending on where data lives. A question to ask; week 22 measures it.
The cost of layers between source and machine. The course authors no Python comparison code.
Cycle counts versus wall-clock time. This course uses POSIX `clock_gettime`.
A budget in cycles; latency versus throughput.
A ballpark estimate before measuring.
The clock contract: POSIX/Linux, not ISO C.
Primary authority for ordering, formatting and time.

E01.title: One executable with clear boundaries
E01.why: Integration exposes differences between an experiment and a reusable interface. The command line has its own grammar and error contract.
E01.predict: Predict which symbols each object should export and how CLI negative zero is normalized.
E01.steps: Reuse the earlier mechanisms behind the supplied headers, keep helpers static, then implement checked CLI parsing and generation. Read the changed file-cleanup rule carefully.
E01.hint: A command-line convenience does not silently change CSV v1's canonical grammar.
E01.evidence: Cross-build byte agreement is evidence about these builds; interface preservation is what lets later weeks replace implementations safely.
E01.prerequisites: Week 3 geometry, Week 4 CSV contracts, and Week 1 linkage

E02.title: Selecting and ordering results
E02.why: A human-readable distance loses precision when printed. Selection and ordering must use the unrounded value if the API is to mean what it says.
E02.predict: Predict the printed-tie fixture's order before reading the output.
E02.steps: Validate the full input, compute each distance once, select inclusively, and sort by distance then identifier. Handle empty success separately from allocation failure.
E02.hint: Subtracting distances and converting the difference to int is not a valid comparator.
E02.evidence: Two identical printed distances need not be an exact tie. Explain the internal ordering and the displayed evidence separately.
E02.prerequisites: unrounded distances, total ordering, validation, and exact versus displayed ties

E03.title: Fixtures that ask a question
E03.why: A good fixture isolates a possible defect. A large random dataset rarely makes the reason for a failure as clear.
E03.predict: Write the expected rows of each tiny fixture before asking the supplied oracle to generate output.
E03.steps: Choose the six required purposes, document each command and defect, then compare expectations, oracle, and program as three distinct artifacts.
E03.hint: Do not create the expected file by capturing the program under test.
E03.evidence: An independent oracle reduces shared implementation mistakes, but still shares the specification and may share assumptions or mathematical limitations.
E03.prerequisites: the checkpoint CLI contract and fixtures that isolate individual validity and ordering rules

E04.title: Defining the timed region
E04.why: A duration is meaningful only when you know exactly which work lies between the clock readings. The three variants answer different questions.
E04.predict: Mark parsing, allocation, arithmetic, hashing, and printing as inside or outside each region.
E04.steps: Implement checked order statistics first. Then bracket the prescribed work, compute checksums after timing, and reject any repetition that changes the result.
E04.hint: Use a difference-based midpoint for an even median; the direct sum may overflow.
E04.evidence: A checksum is evidence of result consistency, not proof that every source-level operation executed.
E04.prerequisites: monotonic elapsed time, explicit timed boundaries, and repetition checks

E05.title: Choosing the experiment in advance
E05.why: It is easy to keep measuring until the result looks pleasing. A written protocol makes the stopping decision independent of the outcome.
E05.predict: Write the number and order of process runs and your stopping rule before collecting data.
E05.steps: Complete PROTOCOL.md, then record dataset identities, builds, repetitions, and environment. Preserve raw outputs instead of retaining only a favored summary.
E05.hint: Interleaving builds helps expose changes over time that would otherwise align with one build.
E05.evidence: Warm caches or scheduling effects are hypotheses here. The protocol does not identify their cause merely by naming them.
E05.prerequisites: the validated benchmark, warm-up, fixed experimental conditions, and a stopping rule

E06.title: Prediction meets measurement
E06.why: A prediction exposes your current model of the work. A mismatch is useful when you can locate the assumption that failed.
E06.predict: Count the math calls and give a cost range before any report timing run.
E06.steps: Preserve the prediction, collect all required medians and spreads, then compare ranges without converting separation into a significance claim.
E06.hint: Read compiler diagnostics before attributing a timing difference to vectorization.
E06.evidence: Different machines can produce different valid rankings. The report must say what these runs establish and what experiment would distinguish explanations.
E06.prerequisites: operation counts, units, medians, spread, and the frozen measurement protocol

E07.title: A checkpoint others can reproduce
E07.why: The baseline is valuable because later changes have something stable to compare against. Packaging the evidence is part of the implementation.
E07.predict: List what a fresh reviewer needs to rebuild, test, and understand the result.
E07.steps: Run the checkpoint, examine its manifest, and complete the report. Resolve failures rather than selecting a passing compiler configuration.
E07.hint: Correctness and explanation are the acceptance criteria; speed is an observation.
E07.evidence: The checkpoint promises this interface and validation evidence. It does not promise identical timings or universal floating-point identity on other platforms.
E07.prerequisites: all checkpoint evidence and the distinction between observation and causal explanation

guidance.P01: Ask what each clock measures and which document promises it. A faster build is an observation; vectorization is a proposed mechanism requiring different evidence.
guidance.P02: Sort a copy of the samples and keep the original order. Compare center and spread with and without the outlier without silently discarding it from the real report.
guidance.P03: Carry the units through every division. The nominal-frequency conversion is an estimate, and the two byte counts describe different accounting conventions.
guidance.P04: Sort the internal values before formatting them. Distinguish an exact tie from two different values that collapse to the same displayed decimal text.
guidance.P05: Follow the CLI stages in order: option syntax, semantic support, file loading, computation, output. Different stages deliberately have different exit codes.
guidance.S01: Stretch: derive file bytes from the distribution rather than guessing an average row size. A byte-rate estimate is not proof that memory bandwidth limits the computation.
guidance.S02: Stretch: use the compiler report as evidence about a particular build. Keep vectorizer availability, attempted transformation, and measured speed separate.
guidance.R01: Copy the environment block from the actual timed build. A machine name alone does not identify compiler flags or clock resolution.
guidance.R02: Complete this section before discussing performance. Explain the input and failure domains covered by each kind of check.
guidance.R03: Freeze the prediction before the data run. Its usefulness comes from exposing a cost model that the measurements can challenge.
guidance.R04: Distinguish variation within one process from variation across processes. Report ambiguous comparisons honestly rather than manufacturing a winner.
guidance.R05: The handoff is the baseline for future changes. Name the exact dataset, build, command, and evidence that make that baseline reproducible.

The toolchain cross-check.

E01.title: Fields inside one byte
E01.why: A byte can contain several small numbers. Extracting each field makes the manual's compact encoding table executable.
E01.predict: Split the four driver bytes on paper and predict which mask removes unrelated high bits.
E01.steps: Draw the field boundaries, shift to position zero, mask, then reassemble the fields to check the decomposition.
E01.hint: Shifting right by three alone leaves the original top two bits in the result.
E01.evidence: The full 256-byte check covers this finite field split, not all later decoder behavior.
E01.prerequisites: unsigned byte values, masks, shifts, and available input length

E02.title: Register names depend on context
E02.why: Field value four does not name one universal register. Width selects the table that gives the field meaning.
E02.predict: Predict both names for register code four and sketch the halves of ax.
E02.steps: Validate width and index before looking up a name. Keep the 8086 tables separate from the modern x86-64 comparison.
E02.hint: ah belongs to ax; it is not an 8-bit version of sp.
E02.evidence: A shared opcode ancestry does not make an 8086 decoder suitable for modern compiler output.
E02.prerequisites: width-dependent register tables and the meaning of each three-bit code

E03.title: Bytes into immediate values
E03.why: The input encoding determines byte order. Your host's representation should not be asked to guess it.
E03.predict: Read 34 12 by hand and predict the signed interpretation of the FE pattern at both widths.
E03.steps: Validate the remaining byte count with subtraction, assemble the unsigned magnitude, then interpret the sign using wider arithmetic.
E03.hint: Prove the read fits before indexing; avoid computing an overflowing offset plus size.
E03.evidence: Host-independent arithmetic decoding and host byte inspection solve different problems, even though both involve bytes.
E03.prerequisites: little-endian arithmetic, field width, and explicit signed interpretation

E04.title: One instruction, one transaction
E04.why: A decoder must decide what it knows before touching the next byte. An ordered status policy makes partial and unsupported inputs predictable.
E04.predict: Trace a valid instruction and each truncation of it through the status order.
E04.steps: Recognize the form, check required fields, validate mode and operation, then read immediates. Build a temporary instruction and commit only on success.
E04.hint: A recognized memory mode is outside this week's subset; rejecting it is more accurate than guessing a length.
E04.evidence: Exhaustive prefixes strongly test status order, but longer immediates still require their own coverage.
E04.prerequisites: opcode fields, ModR/M, instruction lengths, and transactional failure

E05.title: Text is a chosen representation
E05.why: Several byte sequences can mean the same instruction. Printing a canonical form makes comparisons useful without promising recovery of the original encoding.
E05.predict: Derive the longest possible printed instruction before running the formatter.
E05.steps: Validate the instruction object, format into a local bounded buffer, check the reported length, then copy the complete result.
E05.hint: snprintf's return value describes the required length, not only the characters that fit.
E05.evidence: Text equality is semantic agreement under the course convention, not byte identity after reassembly.
E05.prerequisites: decoded instruction fields, canonical syntax, and text-buffer capacity

E06.title: A whole stream or an error
E06.why: A late bad instruction must not leave a plausible partial output that looks successful. Stream decoding therefore needs a commit boundary.
E06.predict: Draw both parses of B8 89 D9, starting at offsets zero and one.
E06.steps: First validate and count the complete stream; only then write text. Keep byte offsets distinct from text lengths and distinguish read, decode, and write errors.
E06.hint: The error offset names the beginning of the failing instruction, not necessarily the byte where validation stopped.
E06.evidence: Successful disassembly depends on the chosen start and architecture. A valid-looking decode does not prove the bytes were intended as code.
E06.prerequisites: single-instruction decoding, stream offsets, and validating before output

E07.title: Cases with independent reasons
E07.why: Writing expected instructions by hand tests whether your mental model agrees with the encoding specification. Purposeful cases also probe gaps in broad generated tests.
E07.predict: Complete the five prescribed hand decodings before running any tool.
E07.steps: For each added case, identify the field rule or error boundary it targets. Compare your derivation with the encoding oracle and then with your decoder.
E07.hint: If the oracle rejects your expectation, investigate the derivation before changing the implementation.
E07.evidence: The manual, encoder-style oracle, and objdump have different roles and conventions. Agreement is evidence with stated limits, not a universal proof.
E07.prerequisites: hand decoding, independent encodings, and text equivalence versus byte identity

guidance.P01: Separate the C operations used to decode a pattern from the ISA rule describing that pattern. The host language and the guest architecture are different authorities.
guidance.P02: Partition bytes into named fields before looking up mnemonics. Keep an offset and consumed-length column so a correct name cannot hide an incorrect boundary.
guidance.P03: Work in the encoding direction and search every permitted form. Several forms can produce the same text, so finding one encoding does not prove uniqueness.
guidance.P04: Read only what the available fields establish. Identify the missing addressing rules instead of borrowing a register-mode length for a memory operand.
guidance.P05: Draw two separate byte partitions. A valid opcode found inside an immediate illustrates why starting position is part of a decoder request.
guidance.P06: Keep the original object-file observation distinct from the supplied fallback fixture. The REX prefix changes interpretation and is not an 8086 feature.
guidance.S01: Stretch: draw the current-instruction and next-instruction addresses before adding the displacement. Alias spellings may differ while the target is the same.
guidance.S02: Stretch: enumerate which bytes each comparison actually covers. A test of two-byte prefixes leaves later immediate-byte behavior to additional tests or a proof.
guidance.R01: Record whether the comparison tool supports the guest architecture. A missing tool is a validation limitation, not evidence that the decoder is wrong.
guidance.R02: Keep the hand-decoded fields and longest-text derivation. A correct final mnemonic alone can conceal a mistaken field interpretation.
guidance.R03: Name the ISA and manual table for an encoding claim. A modern x86-64 rule must not silently enter an 8086 explanation.
guidance.R04: Choose at least one convention difference deliberately. Explain semantic agreement without requiring the tools to print identical text.
guidance.R05: Connect one C operation to the exact bits it extracts. End with the addressing information that the next week must add.
